prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock: magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms and its realisation at a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from circuit QED (B004) to the optical lattice clock (B029), crediting Katori and Ye. The reasons are scientific and procedural. Scientifically, I judge B029 on the question I always ask: did it open a regime that is robust and reproduced across laboratories? Magic-wavelength trapping lets thousands of neutral atoms act as one quantum-limited oscillator, and the 10^-18 level has been reached and compared at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, with the many-body (spin-exchange) physics inside the clock understood in detail. That is the kind of control over every physical detail that I value, and the downstream uses (millimetre-scale redshift, bounds on drifting constants, dark-matter searches) are demonstrated and not just promised. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: every member who proposed a B029 configuration named exactly Katori and Ye, with the idea on one side and the realisation to the limit on the other. Procedurally, B004 is my own community. I flagged a possible recusal, four names compete for three places, and the committee is split on which of Blais and Girvin to drop, so I should not be the lone advocate for a candidate whose credit the record does not settle. My view of the science of B004 is unchanged. I simply no longer think it is the right final position for me to carry.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is territorial. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for ion control cover the tools that make optical clocks possible, so a sceptic can call the lattice clock a refinement of an honoured programme, and Eriksson and Olsson put this forcefully. There is also a real attribution tail (Lemonde, Peik and Hollberg on the proposal; Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley, Lemke, Kitagawa and the ion-clock groups on the achievement), and the best ion clocks still compete on accuracy. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so some of the benefit is still prospective. Finally, a committee could prefer a discovery that reveals unexpected behaviour of nature over a superbly characterised measurement, which is the argument for B031.

responses.point: Kroll wants the B029 citation to cover the measurement achievement and the many-body clock, not only the idea, and asks whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree with the wording point. A citation that only says magic-wavelength trapping would honour the idea and leave out Ye's group, who showed that the scheme delivers 10^-18 including the spin-exchange regime. I would keep the two-clause form: the lattice clock concept and its realisation at 10^-18. On waiting for the redefinition, I would not make it a condition. The committee rewards the discovery and demonstration, and the cross-laboratory comparisons already show the result is robust. A redefinition of the second would be a consequence of this work, not a test of it. Kroll's answer to my round-1 point, that adjacency to 2025 is a sequencing issue and not a verdict on merit, is part of why I can accept B029 without feeling I have treated circuit QED unfairly.

responses.point: Lindroth argues B029 is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and she asked in round 1 whether the circuit-QED discovery is the architecture or the downstream processors.
responses.response: On her question to me, I think the discovery in circuit QED is the regime of strong single-photon coupling, but she is right that the weight of the field now sits in engineering of coherence and gates, and that makes the question of what exactly is rewarded harder to answer in one line than for clocks. For B029, I find her distinction persuasive: neither earlier prize covered a many-atom lattice at 10^-18 with controlled collisions and lattice light shifts, so the novelty claim is real. I would only add that the citation should not mention combs or ion control at all, to avoid appearing to re-award them. She notes she may be biased towards precision atomic physics, which is why I would defer to her and Kroll on priority details while testing the physics claims from my side.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B031 and calls B029 more a refinement of precision spectroscopy than a new behaviour of matter, and in round 1 preferred Girvin to Blais for the third circuit-QED slot.
responses.response: I take the refinement charge seriously, but I think it understates what the lattice clock showed: a many-body quantum system whose interactions, including spin-exchange and collective effects, have to be understood and controlled to reach 10^-18, so the clock is itself a platform for studying quantum behaviour. On B031, I agree with her robustness argument (flat bands supported by several calculations, reproduction by many groups), and I keep it as my first alternative. My remaining hesitation is the credit set, where she, Mehlig and Danielsson all acknowledge that Cao, Fatemi and Dean's group are not covered and that Bistritzer sits uneasily in third place. A two-name MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero pair would make me more comfortable. Her Girvin versus Blais point I now treat as moot for me, since I am stepping back from B004.

responses.point: As Chair, Pearce moved to B029 as the configuration the committee can stand behind and asked whether Katori and Ye adequately capture the proposal history and team contributions.
responses.response: I think crediting only Katori and Ye is adequate. The proposal of magic-wavelength trapping in 2001 to 2003 is Katori's, and Ye's group turned it into the 10^-18 benchmark. Lemonde, Peik, Hollberg and the team members made real contributions, but the three-name limit forces a choice and none of the members who studied the candidate has proposed a different pair. I would not ask for an outside assessment to change the names. If the Chair wants one, it should address only whether the Katori idea or the Ye realisation has a stronger competing claim. On the chair's recusal question about me, I confirm that I will take no part in discussion or ballot on B004, and that I have no tie to Katori, Ye or their groups.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B029 last of her eight on novelty and a modest direct benefit to humanity, and prefers B001 with Wrachtrup and Jelezko.
responses.response: Her novelty worry is the one that most deserves a careful answer. My answer is that the lattice clock is a new instrument whose existence changed what can be measured, such as millimetre height differences through the gravitational redshift, and not only a better number. On benefit, I agree it is still modest compared with NV sensing, and I would not lean on applications in the citation. I keep B001 as my second alternative because I agree with her that single-spin detection and control is original and reproducible, and the Wrachtrup and Jelezko pair is the defensible set. I do not see it as stronger than B029 on cross-laboratory robustness at this stage, given that the biological sensing claims are still developing.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which is the main disagreement among the members who ranked B029.
Whether Katori and Ye are the right pair given the proposal history and team contributions, and whether an outside assessment would change that.
Whether a measurement advance should be preferred over a new regime of correlated matter (B031), where I defer to Eriksson and Mehlig on whether the open pairing mechanism is disqualifying.

Whether the committee will want a second part; I do not see a scientific kinship between B029 and the IceCube part proposed by Danielsson and I defer to him and Pearce on whether Halzen alone can be defended.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I am Director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a Chalmers theorist in superconducting circuits, which is the community behind B004. I know several circuit-QED principals through the field, Chalmers hosted 2025 laureates as WACQT guest researchers, and my Chalmers colleagues (Delsing, Wilson, Kockum) work on related waveguide QED. In answer to the chair's question, I will step back from discussion and any ballot on B004 and have not listed it among my alternatives. I have no specific conflict for B029, B031 or B001 beyond ordinary scientific acquaintance with the quantum-technology community.
